title: Panoramic View of the Glacier National Park
line: John H. Renshawe · U.S. Geological Survey · 1914
credit: American Geographical Society Library, UW-Milwaukee
cap: The Survey’s own painter of parks: Renshawe rendered the topographers’ sheets as a single soft-lit panorama, relief without a single contour. It is an oblique view — no honest way to drape it — so it hangs here as the painting it is.

title: Aeroplane View of Glacier National Park
credit: Internet Archive · scan via the David Rumsey Map Collection
cap: “See America First” from an imaginary altitude: the railway’s promotional bird’s-eye, with every hotel and chalet of its park empire drawn in. The perspective is a salesman’s, not a surveyor’s.

title: Guide Map, Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park
credit: American Geographical Society Library, UW-Milwaukee
cap: The mid-century park at a glance — roads, trails, chalets and the Peace Park border — closing the era the 1915 sheet opened.

title: Map of Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park
line: National Park Service brochure fold-out · revised 1937
credit: NPS History eLibrary
cap: The fold-out every 1930s visitor carried: Going-to-the-Sun finally complete, printed by the Geological Survey for the glovebox rather than the drafting table.

title: Lewis and Clark Forest Reserve — Classification of Lands
line: H.B. Ayres · USGS 21st Annual Report, plate III · 1899
credit: U.S. Geological Survey, Publications Warehouse
cap: Before the parks and the forests had their names, Ayres rode the reserves classifying every township by timber and burn — the Bien-lithographed plates are the region’s first land-use cartography.

title: Flathead National Forest
credit: Montana History Portal · University of Montana
cap: The half-inch-to-the-mile forest map of the Swan and Mission country — hachured relief and the township grid, filling the gap between the Glacier sheets and the valley quads.

title: Sectionized Map of the Flathead Indian Reservation
credit: Montana History Portal · Montana Historical Society
cap: The section grid drawn to administer allotment and the 1910 opening of Séliš, Ql̓ispé and Ksanka lands to homesteaders. Cartographically precise; historically, the paperwork of a dispossession. It hangs here so that can be said plainly.

title: Kalispell, Montana — Sanborn sheet 1
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Fire-insurance cartography at one inch to fifty feet: every building in the young county seat, colour-coded by material. Thirty sheets cover the town; this is the index.

title: Big Fork, Montana — the whole town on one sheet
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Bigfork in 1916 fit on a single Sanborn sheet — mill, dam, hotel and the few dozen buildings above the Swan’s mouth.

title: Map of the Yellowstone and Missouri Rivers and Their Tributaries
line: Raynolds Expedition · compiled by F.V. Hayden · 1859–60
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The army’s reconnaissance of the upper Yellowstone, Jim Bridger guiding — and the plateau itself left nearly blank, the last unmapped corner of the territory. Hayden, the expedition’s naturalist, drew this sheet; a decade later he came back and filled in the blank. The “before” of every draped sheet in this gallery.

title: Upper Geyser Basin, Fire Hole River, Wyoming Territory
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The first map of the Old Faithful basin, sketched the summer before the park act passed — each geyser a numbered point, the intervals timed by pocket watch. Congress voted with this survey’s maps and photographs on its desks.

title: Preliminary Geological Map of the Yellowstone National Park
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The territorial survey’s colour geology of the young park — the reading Hague’s folio would redo with better instruments twenty years on. Hang it beside the draped Folio 30 sheet and you can watch the science grow up.

title: City of Tacoma, W.T. — Western Terminus of the N.P.R.R.
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Twelve years after the Northern Pacific chose Commencement Bay — Puyallup homeland — as its Pacific terminus, the young city sells itself with Mount Rainier for a backdrop. The tacoma sheet drapes the country behind this view.

title: Wallace, Idaho — Sanborn sheet 1
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The silver capital of the Coeur d’Alene, block by block, twenty months before the Big Burn of 1910 took a third of the town it so carefully colour-codes.

title: Denver and Rio Grande Railway System
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The narrow gauge that went where standard track could not — over Marshall Pass, down the Animas gorge to Silverton — drawn at the moment the three-foot empire peaked.

title: The Gold and Coal Fields of Alaska, with Steamer Routes and Trails
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The Survey’s answer to Klondike fever: every route north — steamer lanes, passes, winter trails — on one sheet, printed the year before the beach at Nome turned gold.

title: A Map of Lewis and Clark’s Track Across the Western Portion of North America
line: William Clark · engraved by Samuel Lewis · 1814
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The master map of the expedition, drawn by Clark from his own field sheets — the Missouri traced bend by bend past the falls and the Marias, the whole West hung on one river. Every sheet in this gallery descends from it.

title: Land Grant of the Northern Pacific Railroad in Montana and Idaho
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: The checkerboard itself: every odd-numbered section for forty miles either side of the line, the price Congress paid to get the road built — an area larger than some states, drawn as calmly as a timetable.

title: Map of Central Montana — the Montana Railroad
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Richard Harlow’s Montana Railroad, promoted here at its hopeful best — the line they said he financed with his jaw, wandering up Sixteenmile Canyon toward Lewistown. The Milwaukee later bought his bluff and made it a main line.

title: Bird’s Eye View of Missoula, Montana
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Missoula the year after the Northern Pacific arrived — mills on the Clark Fork, the bridge, Hellgate Canyon behind — the town the 1912 quadrangle would later leave just off its eastern edge, drawn here in full.

title: Bird’s Eye View of Livingston, Montana
credit: Library of Congress, Geography & Map Division
cap: Livingston in its first year: the Northern Pacific’s shops and roundhouse, the grid staked into the sagebrush, and the Park Branch curving south toward Paradise Valley — drawn while the paint was still wet on the depot.
